transcript:
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Dave Mattingly.
Iran's foreign minister says he's waiting for a response from the Trump administration
on a proposal to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ship traffic.
Last week, President Trump rejected a seven-day Iranian proposal, which called for the U.S.
to agree to ease its sanctions on Tehran, and PR's Hadil Al-Shalchi reports.
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araxi said he met with Qatari mediators, where they "engaged
in discussions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz."
Araxi said the Qataris relayed Iran's demands to the U.S.
Araxi also suggested Iran expected the Qatari mediators to relay the decision.
Last week at the U.N., Iran said it was ready to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in seven days.
Following the lifting of mutual blockades over the waterway, Iran said it was willing
to sit down for broader talks to end the war and address its nuclear program.
President Trump rejected the latest Iranian proposal, but said he still intends to pursue
negotiations and talk about a broader deal.
Hadil Al-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
The U.S. Navy says two pilots were rescued in the Atlantic yesterday after rejecting
from their plane while attempting to land on an aircraft carrier.
It happened off the coast of Virginia and involved the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower.
The Navy says four sailors aboard the carrier were also injured, none seriously in what
officials are calling a mishap.
It's unclear what led to the failed landing or what type of aircraft was involved.
A bill designed to reform college athletics is heading to the House now that it's cleared
the Senate.
The Protect College Sports Act cleared the Senate on a vote of 77 to 22.
NPR's Becky Sullivan has more.
Supporters of the bill say it's needed to curtail chaos in college sports, where lawsuits
have chipped away at longstanding NCAA rules around amateurism, transfers, and eligibility.
The legislation would give the NCAA a limited antitrust exemption in order to restore some
of those rules.
Critics felt it didn't go far enough to rein in other runaway spending on things like recruiting
and facilities and coaching salaries.
This was a bipartisan bill with bipartisan opposition.
Yays and nays came from Republicans and Democrats alike.
In a statement, NCAA President Charlie Baker thanked senators but noted there's still
much work left to do.
The bill is supported by President Trump, but first it must pass the House, which has
gone on recess until after the midterms.
Becky Sullivan in PR News.
A county prosecutor in New York says he's reopening an investigation into allegations
that seven students at Cornell University sexually assaulted a woman at a fraternity
house nearly two years ago.
This follows a lawsuit being filed by the woman who alleges the attack took place at
an on-campus frat house after she was pressured into drinking alcohol, smoking marijuana,
and snorting ketamine.
This is NPR News.
It's been nearly eight months since the mother of NBC Today show host Savannah Guthrie was
reported missing from her home in Arizona.
Nancy Guthrie has not been located and no suspects have been arrested, but authorities
say they're looking into the possibility of a new ransom note.
That's according to the Pima County Sheriff's Department.
Investigators say they're working to determine the note's credibility.
Lindsey Clancy is due back in a Massachusetts courtroom today for the first time since a
mistrial was declared in her murder case.
Clancy had been charged with killing her three children.
Deborah Becker with member station WBUR says a hearing is being held to determine if Clancy
will be retried.
Clancy's defense has filed a flurry of motions, including one to dismiss the case.
The defense argues that the judge didn't have to declare a mistrial and should have investigated
reports that one of the 12 jurors wasn't following the law.
Retired judge Jack Lew doesn't expect any quick decisions on the motions.
I would think the most likely scenario is people ask for time to address these issues.
Prosecutors have not said if they'll seek a new trial on first-degree murder charges
or try to negotiate a plea deal.
For NPR News, I'm Deborah Becker in Boston.
SpaceX says it shortened yesterday's test launch of its giant Starship rocket after
one of the main engines failed.
The 407-foot rocket reached orbit for the first time after launching from Texas and
circled the Earth three times instead of the Plan 6.
Starship also released 26 Starlink satellites.
I'm Dave Mattingly, NPR News, in Washington.

topics.text: Iran's foreign minister waits for Trump administration response on reopening Strait of Hormuz
U.S. Navy rescues two pilots after ejecting from plane near USS Dwight D. Eisenhower
Protect College Sports Act clears Senate 77-22, heads to House for consideration
New York county prosecutor reopens investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University fraternity
Nancy Guthrie, mother of NBC Today show host Savannah Guthrie, remains missing from Arizona
Lindsey Clancy returns to Massachusetts court as judge considers motions in murder case mistrial
SpaceX shortens Starship test launch after engine failure, reaches orbit and deploys Starlink satellites
